questions.title: Coupled carts and a buffer spring
questions.subtopic: Coupled carts and a buffer spring
questions.stem: A $1.20\,\mathrm{kg}$ cart moves at $3.00\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ and couples to a stationary $0.800\,\mathrm{kg}$ cart on a horizontal track. External impulse during the $0.0500\,\mathrm s$ coupling is negligible. The coupled carts then compress an initially unstretched ideal spring of constant $180\,\mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$. Resistance after the collision is negligible.

questions.title: Insulating a cold-room wall
questions.stem: A wall of area $12.0\,\mathrm{m^2}$, thickness $0.200\,\mathrm m$ and thermal conductivity $0.800\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ separates air at $22.0^\circ\mathrm C$ from air at $2.0^\circ\mathrm C$. Treat the wall surfaces as being at these temperatures. An insulating layer of thickness $0.0500\,\mathrm m$ and conductivity $0.0400\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ is added to the cold side. Assume steady one-dimensional conduction and no other losses. The heater converts $80.0\%$ of electrical input into useful room heating.

sourceAnchors.focus: Wall conduction with new insulation and an electrical-energy comparison

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe conduction in the solid wall at the particle level.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the heat-transfer rate through the bare wall.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the heat-transfer rate after insulation is added.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Calculate the wall-insulation interface temperature.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Calculate the electrical energy saved in $10.0\,\mathrm h$, in $\mathrm{kWh}$.

steps.text: Particles at the hot side have greater mean random vibrational energy and transfer energy to neighbouring particles through interactions.
There is net energy transfer down the temperature gradient without bulk motion of the solid; free electrons can also carry energy in a conducting material.
The wall drop is $PL_1/(k_1A)=3.33\,\mathrm K$, so the interface is $22.0-3.33=18.7^\circ\mathrm C$.
Input power saved is $(960-160)/0.800=1000\,\mathrm W=1.00\,\mathrm{kW}$, so energy saved is $10.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

questions.answerSummary: (a) There is net energy transfer down the temperature gradient without bulk motion of the solid; free electrons can also carry energy in a conducting material.; (b) $P=960\,\mathrm W$.; (c) $P=12.0(20.0)/(0.200/0.800+0.0500/0.0400)=160\,\mathrm W$.; (d) The wall drop is $PL_1/(k_1A)=3.33\,\mathrm K$, so the interface is $22.0-3.33=18.7^\circ\mathrm C$.; (e) Input power saved is $(960-160)/0.800=1000\,\mathrm W=1.00\,\mathrm{kW}$, so energy saved is $10.0\,\mathrm{kWh}$.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Explain why a fixed phase relationship between the slits is required for a stable fringe pattern.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the separation of adjacent bright fringes.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the distance between the first dark fringe to the left of the central maximum and the second dark fringe to its right.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The entire slit-screen region is filled with a transparent medium of refractive index $1.33$. Calculate the new bright-fringe separation and explain the change.

steps.text: A stable phase difference lets the same positions retain constructive or destructive interference.
If the phase difference changes randomly, bright and dark positions move rapidly and the time-averaged pattern washes out.
Dark positions are at half-integer fringe spacings. The requested positions are $-0.5s$ and $+1.5s$.
Frequency is unchanged while speed and wavelength are reduced by factor $1.33$, so fringe spacing is also divided by $1.33$.

questions.answerSummary: (a) If the phase difference changes randomly, bright and dark positions move rapidly and the time-averaged pattern washes out.; (b) $s=5.00\,\mathrm{mm}$.; (c) The separation is $2s=10.0\,\mathrm{mm}$.; (d) $s_{\rm new}=5.00/1.33=3.76\,\mathrm{mm}$.

questions.title: Does a proton leave the deflector?

Use proton charge $1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm C$ and mass $1.67\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$.

parts.prompt: Calculate the proton acceleration.

parts.prompt: Assuming it could travel the full plate length, calculate its vertical displacement by the exit plane.

parts.label: d

steps.text: Horizontal speed is unchanged, so $t=L/v_x=3.00\times10^{-7}\,\mathrm s$.
The available upward clearance from the entry midpoint is only $0.0200\,\mathrm m$, less than the projected displacement.

The proton therefore hits the upper plate before the exit plane; the unimpeded trajectory used in (c) cannot describe motion beyond contact. Accept the equivalent calculation $x_{\rm hit}=0.0264\,\mathrm m<0.0300\,\mathrm m$.

questions.answerSummary: (a) $F=qE=9.60\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm N$, upward.; (b) $a=5.75\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, upward.; (c) $y=\tfrac12at^2=0.0259\,\mathrm m$.; (d) The proton therefore hits the upper plate before the exit plane; the unimpeded trajectory used in (c) cannot describe motion beyond contact. Accept the equivalent calculation $x_{\rm hit}=0.0264\,\mathrm m<0.0300\,\mathrm m$.

questions.title: An activated sample above background
questions.stem: An activated sample undergoes beta-minus decay, forming a stable daughter. Its initial parent-nucleus count is $8.00\times10^9$. A detector has a constant background rate $30.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$. Its expected gross count rates are $270\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $t=0$ and $90.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ at $t=20.0\,\mathrm{min}$. Detector efficiency remains constant. The illustrative curve shows expected rates rather than individual random measurements.

sourceAnchors.focus: Background-corrected half-life inference and random-count interpretation

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: For a parent ${}^{A}_{Z}X$, write the beta-minus decay equation with a daughter Y and all emitted particles.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Determine the sample half-life.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict the gross count rate at $30.0\,\mathrm{min}$.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Determine the number of parent nuclei remaining at $30.0\,\mathrm{min}$.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Explain why a short measured count rate need not lie exactly on the curve and can occasionally be below the expected background rate.

steps.text: The daughter has nucleon number $A$ and proton number $Z+1$.
${}^{A}_{Z}X\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}Y+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu_e$. An electron antineutrino accompanies the beta-minus electron.
Subtract background: source rates are $240$ and $60.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, a reduction by $4$.
This is two half-lives in $20.0\,\mathrm{min}$, so $T_{1/2}=10.0\,\mathrm{min}$.
After three half-lives the source rate is $240/8=30.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$.
Radioactive detection and background events are random, so finite-interval counts fluctuate around their expected values.

The expected background is a mean, not a strict lower bound on a measured short-interval count rate; sufficiently long averages approach the expected curve. No negative physical source rate is implied.

questions.answerSummary: (a) ${}^{A}_{Z}X\to{}^{A}_{Z+1}Y+{}^{0}_{-1}e+\bar\nu_e$. An electron antineutrino accompanies the beta-minus electron.; (b) This is two half-lives in $20.0\,\mathrm{min}$, so $T_{1/2}=10.0\,\mathrm{min}$.; (c) Add background to obtain $60.0\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ gross.; (d) $N=8.00\times10^9/8=1.00\times10^9$ parent nuclei.; (e) The expected background is a mean, not a strict lower bound on a measured short-interval count rate; sufficiently long averages approach the expected curve. No negative physical source rate is implied.

Use $\sigma=5.67\times10^{-8}\,\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}\,K^{-4}}$, Wien constant $2.90\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm{m\,K}$ and $1\,\mathrm{pc}=3.086\times10^{16}\,\mathrm m$.

steps.text: Inward gravitational attraction is balanced by an outward pressure gradient in hydrostatic equilibrium.
Energy from core fusion helps maintain the temperature and pressure; energy transported outward is radiated from the surface, allowing approximate equilibrium over main-sequence timescales.
